Retail Trading Platforms Post Record Quarters as Investor Apps Multiply

VANCOUVER, BC, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Wall Street Investor News Commentary - Four publicly listed retail investing platforms now report more than 41 million funded accounts between them, and two of them reported record quarters this summer. The pattern is the same across all of them: more people are managing their own money from a phone, and the platforms competing for them are adding research, data and AI tools alongside the trade button. Active Companies from around the markets include: Robinhood Markets, Inc. (NASDAQ: HOOD), Webull Corporation (NASDAQ: BULL), Futu Holdings Limited (NASDAQ: FUTU), eToro Group Ltd. (NASDAQ: ETOR), Morningstar, Inc. (NASDAQ: MORN).

Not every investor needs a brokerage to follow the market. A growing set of free tools sits one step before the trade, built for people who want to watch prices, understand why a stock moved and keep a watchlist without paying for a terminal. Those tools now compete on the same features the brokerages use to win accounts: live quotes, plain-language explanations and AI research.

Quote Daddy is one of them. It is a free stock-tracking app for the web, iPhone and Android with live watchlists for U.S. stocks and ETFs, interactive charts, insider activity from SEC Form 4 filings, alerts, and one-tap AI briefings that explain in plain English why a stock moved. There is no credit card and no paywall; accounts are free at quotedaddy.com.

In other industry developments and happenings in the market this week include:

Robinhood Markets, Inc. (NASDAQ: HOOD)

Robinhood reported record second quarter 2026 revenue of $1.31 billion, up 32% from a year earlier. Funded customers rose 7% to 28.4 million, total platform assets rose 32% to $369 billion, and Robinhood Gold subscribers grew 39% to 4.8 million. Net deposits were $21.7 billion for the quarter, and the company has scheduled its third quarter results for October 27.

Webull Corporation (NASDAQ: BULL)

Webull reported second quarter 2026 revenue of $198.8 million, up 51% year over year, and net income attributable to the company of $24.4 million, compared with a net loss a year earlier. Registered users rose 13% to 28.2 million, funded accounts rose 8% to 5.13 million, and customer assets climbed 79% to $28.5 billion.

"I'm proud to report a record second quarter for Webull," said CEO Anthony Denier, who credited the rollout of updated active-trader features after the elimination of the Pattern Day Trader rule on June 4.

Futu Holdings Limited (NASDAQ: FUTU)

Futu, the parent of the moomoo investing app, reported second quarter 2026 total revenues of US$918.2 million, up 35.6% year over year, and net income of US$464.4 million, up 41.6%. Funded accounts grew 33.6% to 3,842,667, registered users reached 31.3 million, and client assets rose 43.6% to HK$1.40 trillion.

"Malaysia led new funded account additions for the third consecutive quarter," said Leaf Hua Li, Chairman and CEO.

eToro Group Ltd. (NASDAQ: ETOR)

eToro, which combines trading with a social investing feed, reported second quarter 2026 net contribution of $229 million, up 9% year over year, and GAAP net income of $53 million, up 77%. Funded accounts rose 18% to 4.28 million and assets under administration grew 10% to $19.2 billion.

"We delivered another strong quarter as we continue executing against our long-term strategy," said Yoni Assia, Co-Founder and CEO.

Morningstar, Inc. (NASDAQ: MORN)

Morningstar, the investment research and data provider, reported second quarter 2026 revenue of $663.2 million, up 9.6%, and operating income of $160.6 million, up 28.4%. Revenue from its Morningstar Direct platform rose 6.2% to $222.1 million and PitchBook revenue rose 4.9% to $174.7 million.

"We are continuing to deliver profitable growth with meaningful increases in operating and free cash flows," said CEO Kunal Kapoor. Morningstar plans to report third quarter results on October 28.

data.title: AI Revenue Questions Pull Semiconductor Stocks Off October Highs
data.description:
AI Revenue Questions Pull Semiconductor Stocks Off October Highs

AI Revenue Questions Pull Semiconductor Stocks Off October Highs

PR Newswire

VANCOUVER, BC, Oct. 10, 2026

VANCOUVER, BC, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Stock Preachers News Commentary - Semiconductor equities began October on firm footing, with the iShares Semiconductor ETF advancing for five consecutive sessions and the sector's largest company reaching a record high, before retreating through the week ended October 9. Sentiment shifted on Thursday, when the Financial Times reported that OpenAI had told investors its annualized revenue was nearing $50 billion at the end of September, below the approximately $70 billion figure that had been cited in media reports. Because semiconductor valuations are closely tied to expectations for AI infrastructure spending, the report weighed on the group, and the PHLX Semiconductor Index finished the week lower while the broader market was more resilient. Active Companies from around the markets with current developments this week include: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE: TSM), NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA), Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC), Arm Holdings plc (NASDAQ: ARM), Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MU).

The pullback follows a period of substantial gains. The PHLX Semiconductor Index was up 73% year to date as of late September, and several of the sector's largest constituents have recorded triple-digit gains in 2026. Higher long-term Treasury yields and a rise in crude oil prices added pressure midweek, as higher discount rates tend to weigh most on companies valued on long-term growth expectations.

Company-specific developments shaped performance within the group. Two companies reported record milestones early in the week, while others faced open questions regarding a manufacturing partnership, ongoing litigation and the sustainability of AI-related demand.

CONTINUED... Read the full weekly market analysis in The Roadmap at: stockpreachers.com

In other industry developments and happenings in the market this week include:

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company Limited (NYSE: TSM)

TSMC shares reached a record high on October 5 after Elon Musk confirmed early-stage discussions about a role for the company in his planned Terafab chip complex in Texas, calling them "just discussions." On October 8 the company reported September revenue of NT$511.86 billion, up 54.6% from a year earlier and down 0.6% from August, bringing revenue for the first nine months of 2026 to NT$3.90 trillion, up 41.1%.

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA)

NVIDIA shares reached a record high on October 5, bringing their year-to-date gain to approximately 24.8% and their advance since the August 26 earnings report to approximately 14%. The company has also shown relative strength during recent sector weakness: on September 28, when semiconductor shares declined on AI safety concerns, NVIDIA advanced after announcing a $150 billion share buyback authorization and releasing two open-source tools designed to help control AI agents.

Intel Corporation (NASDAQ: INTC)

Intel shares declined on October 5 after Musk indicated that TSMC could participate in Terafab, a project Intel joined as a partner in April. On October 8 Musk said his companies will build and operate the Texas complex and that another chipmaker could at most sublease part of the site. Intel has said it will remain involved, although the scope of its role has not been finalized. Despite the decline, Intel shares were up approximately 215% year to date as of the October 5 close.

Arm Holdings plc (NASDAQ: ARM)

Arm shares declined during a five-day jury trial in federal court in Wilmington, Delaware, where Qualcomm alleges that Arm breached their licensing agreements and sought to undermine Qualcomm's dealings with Meta Platforms. Arm denies the claims. The case went to the jury on October 9, and the judge has not yet ruled on whether a clause that could let Qualcomm stop paying royalties for five years is enforceable. Arm reports earnings on November 4.

Micron Technology, Inc. (NASDAQ: MU)

Micron shares declined alongside other memory producers despite Rosenblatt raising its price target to $1,900 from $1,500 on October 6, citing a beat-and-raise quarter and the potential for buybacks. Memory producers had advanced with the broader group in early October before sentiment shifted later in the week.

data.title: Elon Musk is now richer than any American ever - and it's not even close
data.description:
By Christine Ji

Musk's trillioniare status means he's wealthier than his next three contemporaries combined - and also worth more than historical tycoons like John D. Rockefeller

Elon Musk's fortune eclipses that of any other American in history when tracked by how their wealth compares to U.S. GDP at the time.

Recent gains in shares of SpaceX and Tesla have pushed Elon Musk's net worth back beyond the trillion-dollar mark.

Musk's wealth has earned him the title of the world's first and only trillionaire - and the richest person in the history of America by certain measures, surpassing the wealth of industrialists like John D. Rockefeller and Andrew Carnegie when looking relative to economic output.

As of Thursday, Musk's net worth was $1.02 trillion, according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index. The majority of Musk's wealth comes from his stakes in SpaceX (SPCX) and Tesla (TSLA), two companies with multi-trillion-dollar market capitalizations. Since the beginning of the month, shares of both companies have risen 6%.

Musk holds a 48.4% equity stake in SpaceX, which represents approximately 6.42 billion shares across common stock, options and unvested performance awards, according to an August SEC filing. Musk also owns 20% of Tesla, according to a June SEC filing. However, wealth calculations typically exclude the value of unvested performance shares. Musk also owns shares of his private companies Neuralink and the Boring Co.

These positions make Musk's net worth highly volatile. His wealth peaked at $1.32 trillion in June following SpaceX's IPO but then fell below $700 billion in August as those shares lost ground.

Despite these fluctuations, Musk has solidly established himself as the wealthiest person in the world, both now and compared to previous eras.

Musk's current net worth makes him richer than the world's next three wealthiest individuals - Google (GOOG) (GOOGL) co-founder Larry Page, Amazon.com (AMZN) founder Jeff Bezos and and Google co-founder Sergey Brin - combined.

Musk has spent the majority of the past five years in the top position since first overtaking Bezos in 2021. Musk's current trillionaire status is also a testament to how much the ceiling for wealth has expanded in the past few years. In 2020, Bezos became the first person to ever cross the $200 billion mark. In April 2025, Musk's net worth of $342 billion made him the wealthiest person in the world. In the 18 months since, Musk's net worth has nearly tripled.

Musk also remains peerless when compared to the richest Americans in history.

The industrialists of the 19th and 20th centuries made their fortunes on new markets like oil, steel and railroads. Today, the artificial-intelligence boom has drawn comparisons to the Industrial Revolution in terms of the transformative potential of the technology. While the economic impact of AI has yet to fully emerge, Musk has already surpassed the richest Americans in history in terms of his relative share of gross domestic output.

MarketWatch identified comparable historic figures from Forbes' 2007 list of the richest Americans of all time, then calculated each individual's peak net worth as a percentage of U.S. GDP at the time. Those historical GDP shares were then applied to today's economy.

U.S. GDP reached an annualized $32.56 trillion in the second quarter ending Sept. 30. That means Musk's fortune equates to roughly 3.1% of the entire national economy - a higher percentage than any American before him.

Measuring historic wealth by modern-day standards is challenging because the underlying economic conditions have changed drastically. Additionally, readers should note that historical net-worth estimates are often debated due to differences in record-keeping and varying valuation methods. With that being said, economists typically measure historic wealth as a share of GDP instead of adjusting by standard consumer price inflation.

For example, Standard Oil founder John D. Rockefeller has long been considered the richest American in history. Rockefeller was worth $900 million at his peak in 1913, according to biographer Ron Chernow. Adjusted for inflation, his fortune would be worth $30.4 billion today. But when compared to U.S. GDP in 1913 - which was $39.5 billion, according to Measuring Worth - Rockefeller's wealth comprised 2.3% of total national output, or the equivalent of roughly $742 billion in today's economy.

Andrew Carnegie is believed to have given away $350 million, or roughly 90% of his fortune, over his lifetime. But to pinpoint his net worth at a specific point in time, MarketWatch used the 1901 buyout of Carnegie Steel to J.P Morgan as a benchmark for his peak wealth. While the exact amount is debated, PBS claims Carnegie walked away from the transaction with $250 million, earning him the title of the richest man in the world at the time. The proceeds of the sale represented 1.1% of U.S. GDP at the time, or the equivalent of $355 billion today.

-Christine Ji

data.title: Korean Cultural Center New York Presents "Tchah Sup Kim: The Key to a New World," Featuring an Artwork on Loan from MoMA
data.description:
Korean Cultural Center New York Presents "Tchah Sup Kim: The Key to a New World," Featuring an Artwork on Loan from MoMA

Korean Cultural Center New York Presents "Tchah Sup Kim: The Key to a New World," Featuring an Artwork on Loan from MoMA

PR Newswire

NEW YORK, Oct. 9, 2026

The Artist's First Posthumous Retrospective Showcases More Than 130 Works and Archival Materials

On view September 17 - October 24, 2026 
Gallery & Atrium at the Korean Cultural Center New York

NEW YORK, Oct. 9, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- The Korean Cultural Center New York (KCCNY) presents Tchah Sup Kim: The Key to a New World, a retrospective of Korean artist Tchah Sup Kim (1940–2022), on view through October 24, 2026, in KCCNY's Gallery and Atrium.

Featuring more than 130 works and archival materials spanning nearly five decades, the exhibition traces Kim's artistic and intellectual journey between New York and Korea, from his early printmaking experiments in the 1970s to later works exploring civilization, history, nature, and the cosmos.

Major New York institutions hold Kim's work, including The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), The Metropolitan Museum of Art, and the Brooklyn Museum. His work was also featured in the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum's 2023 exhibition Only the Young: Experimental Art in Korea, 1960s–1970s.

"New York was not simply a place where Tchah Sup Kim lived and worked; it was where his visual language and way of thinking expanded," said Hee Sung Cho, Curator and Program Director of Visual Arts at KCCNY. "Through this exhibition, we hope to show his lifelong search for new ways of perceiving and understanding the world."

New York: Shaping an Artistic Vision

Kim moved to New York in 1974 with support from the John D. Rockefeller 3rd Fund Fellowship and went on to study printmaking at Pratt Institute, where he developed a distinctive visual language through etching.

Among the works on view is Triangle Between Infinities (1976), on loan from The Museum of Modern Art. The work introduced the triangle as a recurring motif in Kim's practice. By opening one vertex of the geometric form, Kim transformed the triangle from a closed structure into one suggesting openness, circulation, and connection.

While geometry played an important role in his early work, Kim's practice increasingly reflected his experience of living between cultures. During the 1980s, his self-portraits explored the displacement and cultural tension he felt as an immigrant artist in New York.

The Coffee Cup Series: An Everyday Object, Reimagined

A centerpiece of the exhibition is Kim's Coffee Cup Series, created between 1984 and 1989 and presented together in its entirety.

The series began with the flattened form of the familiar Greek-style paper coffee cup associated with New York diners. Kim transformed this everyday object into a surface for images, symbols, figures, and language, using an icon of American popular culture to reflect on migration, identity, and his experience of New York life.

The exhibition brings together all 85 works from the series, allowing visitors to see the subtle variations of imagery and language that emerged within its repeated format.

Inside the Artist's SoHo Studio

The exhibition also recreates part of the SoHo studio where Kim lived and worked with his wife and fellow artist Myong-Hi Kim beginning in 1982.

An unfinished painting and easel are displayed alongside objects from the artist's working environment—including globes, rulers, books, stones, a baseball, and natural materials that became recurring sources of inspiration in his work.

The recreated studio offers a glimpse into Kim's creative process and the environment in which his artistic and philosophical ideas developed over decades.

After returning to Korea in the 1990s, Kim's interests expanded from personal experiences of migration and identity toward broader questions of civilization, history, geography, astronomy, and human existence. His later works drew on subjects ranging from Eurasian cultures and historical geography to the structures of the universe, continuing his lifelong search for ways of seeing beyond established systems of thought.

The exhibition title, The Key to a New World, comes from a phrase found in one of Kim's own notes. For Kim, a "new world" was not simply an imagined future, but the possibility of seeing and thinking beyond existing frameworks.

About the Artist

Tchah Sup Kim received his BFA from Seoul National University in 1963. With support from the John D. Rockefeller 3rd Fund Fellowship, he moved to New York in 1974 and received his MFA from Pratt Institute in 1976.

Working primarily in painting and mixed media, Kim explored the cosmos through nature and natural phenomena, raising fundamental questions about humanity's enduring search for universal truths.

His artistic journey can be divided into three major periods: from 1965 to 1982, during his early years in Korea and New York, his work was characterized by a focus on geometry; from 1983 to 1993, during his New York period, he turned toward geopolitical and historical themes; and from 1993 to 2022, after leaving New York for the rural village of Naepyung-ri in Korea and later alternating between the two locations, he focused on geography and nature.

About the Korean Cultural Center New York

Established in 1979, KCCNY is a branch of the Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism of the Republic of Korea dedicated to promoting Korean arts and culture in New York. It presents a wide range of cultural programs, including exhibitions, performing arts, film, and educational programs.

Located at 122 E 32nd Street in New York, near Manhattan's Koreatown, KCCNY serves as a cultural hub in the heart of the city. The seven-story center offers audiences opportunities to experience Korea's rich heritage and dynamic contemporary culture while fostering dialogue, creativity, and cross-cultural exchange.

For more information, visit www.koreanculture.org and follow @kccny on Instagram.

For inquiries: Dr. Bora Yoon (Manager, Visual Arts), b.yoon@koreanculture.org

Media Assets: Access the press kit for the official event poster and exhibition photos.

data.title: A friend in her 80s fell down her basement stairs. Is this a hidden danger lurking in people's home?
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'She developed pleural effusion - fluid between the lungs and ribs - compressing her lungs and making it hard for her to breathe'

"My aunt had a stairlift installed when severe arthritis made the stairs dangerous." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

I read the letter from the 80-year-old reader who wondered whether he should renovate or downsize ('I have $400,000 in equity': I'm 80. Should I sell my house because of dangerous stairs - or spend thousands renovating?).

Here's a cautionary tale, which your readers may find of interest in light of that story. A friend in her 80s slipped on the stairs to her flooded basement and fell, breaking two posterior ribs and injuring her shoulder.

The pain was excruciating. She developed pleural effusion - fluid between the lungs and ribs - compressing her lungs and making it hard for her to breathe. A chest tube was inserted to drain the fluid.

Her sister traveled from out of state to help, and once my friend can travel, she will convalesce with her family in another state. She faces months of healing and rehabilitation to get back to full health.

My aunt had a stairlift installed for her steep staircase when severe arthritis made the stairs dangerous for her. There are many options for the person in question to consider. It's wise to take dangerous stairs seriously.

Forevery Wary About Stairs

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

Related: My wife never went back to work after raising our kids. Do I have to share my retirement savings 50/50?

People do put stairlifts into basement stairwells, but when cost is an issue, choices need to be made.

Dear Wary,

A stairlift can be a lifesaver for millions of older adults. It can also be expensive.

People do put stairlifts into basement stairwells, but the steeper and narrower space can make them trickier and possibly more expensive to install. Depending on the configuration of the stairs, it may be more practical to install a stairlift on the main staircase, which is often the most heavily used set of stairs in the house. Your friend was unlucky that she took a tumble on those basement stairs. If in doubt about stairs, older people should wait for a friend or family member, but it's also easier to lecture people after the fact.

If you have reduced mobility, stairlifts are an effective way to remain in your house. Government grants, veterans' benefits and local programs can help with the cost. What happened to your friend is an all-too-common occurrence, and Medicare can foot the cost for necessary inpatient rehab, as long as its eligibility requirements are met. A fall can lead to broken bones, and remaining sedentary for weeks or months while recovering can have a domino effect on a senior's health.

There are a couple of understandable reasons older people put off installing a stairlift. They might also hesitate to install a shower chair or add handrails at the front door for all the neighbors to see. These things are an acknowledgement to others and to yourself that you're getting older. And stairlifts, notwithstanding any grants, are not cheap. They can cost anywhere from $5,000 to $15,000 to install, depending on the brand and the stairwell.

Related: 'We lived within our means': I earned $30,000 as a pastor and still retired comfortably. Why don't you tell people that?

Falls can be traumatic and even fatal

For anyone in a similar situation, before deciding to sell a house you love, consider whether relatively modest changes can make it safe enough to remain there - and whether the house can continue to work for you if your mobility declines further. Such changes will vary in cost and might mean adding a stairlift, better lighting, handrails, nonslip surfaces, a safer bathroom or even relocating a bedroom to the main floor.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has some startling statistics. Every year, there are roughly 4.5 million visits to emergency rooms due to elderly people falling, resulting in 3.1 million treated and released and 1.4 million hospitalizations (falls account for 88% of emergency-room visits for hip fractures among older adults). Falls are the most common cause of traumatic brain injuries for older adults and result in around 43,000 fatalities every year.

Falls are the most common cause of traumatic brain injuries for older adults.

Staircases are a flashpoint for accidents in general. More than 1 million people visit ERs each year for stair-related injuries, with young children and older adults more likely to injure themselves this way, according to a study published in the American Journal of Emergency Medicine. Women are injured more often than men. Older adults are also more likely to suffer fractures, while younger children are more likely to sustain head and neck injuries.

As well as broken or uneven steps, weak ankles or knees and inappropriate footwear, a variety of other factors can lead to falls, the CDC says. Those include lower-body weakness; vitamin D deficiency; age-related balance and mobility issues (especially after a period of illness or, say, a pandemic); side effects of prescription drugs like tranquilizers, sedatives or antidepressants; and even some over-the-counter medicines such as antihistamines and sleep aids.

Don't miss: 'We made a bad, bad decision': I learned the hard way how to manage my aging father's money

Psychological and physical independence

And, yes, the desire to do things yourself is understandable, if sometimes regrettable. Why wait for the housekeeper to make that trip to the garden shed for hedge clippers? Why ask someone else to climb a stepladder to reach a cobweb? We all take chances, sometimes without thinking about the cumulative risk. A fall can rob older people of the very independence that they are trying to preserve by carrying out those tasks.

As your friend's experience illustrates, when an older person falls, the effects can be long-lasting, and not just physically. I recently saw an elderly woman fall at a book signing. She tripped backwards over a wooden platform, and I was surprised that she was able to get up, but the biggest surprise was how it affected her emotionally. She had had a fright and could not even deal with the concern and empathy of onlookers.

In addition to the complications your friend endured, a bad fall can lead to loss of mobility and even a possible withdrawal from social situations due to fear of falling again. You may endure a period of time where you cannot put your own clothes, bathe, or even cook or feed yourself. With or without other age-related medical conditions like heart disease, hypertension, frailty or Parkinson's disease, you may experience a psychological as well as a physical spiral.

A stairlift can help preserve your independence, but it's only one part of the solution.

data.title: 'I have no children': My aunt gave me $50,000 for a down payment. Now she wants me to leave my home to her two children.
data.description:
By Quentin Fottrell

'The house cost $385,000. With my savings, her $50,000 and a small mortgage, I was able to close.'

"I've always planned for whatever I leave to go to my brother, a dear friend and a couple of charities I care about." (Photo subject is a model.)

Dear Quentin,

Eleven years ago, my aunt gave me $50,000 toward my house, and I'm still grateful. I was 44, newly divorced and buying my first home on my own. I had about $65,000 saved but was short on the down payment for a three-bedroom in a neighborhood I liked. My aunt had money in a savings account earning next to nothing, and she said she'd rather see it go toward a home. She called it a gift and never asked me to sign anything.

The house cost $385,000. With my savings, her $50,000 and a small mortgage, I was able to close. Since then I've put in about $90,000 more: a new roof, kitchen appliances, plumbing work and new windows. The house is worth around $650,000 now, though that isn't cash in my pocket, and I still owe about $180,000. My aunt is 78 and has two adult children, a son,52, and a daughter, 49.

I barely know them. We see each other at Thanksgiving and Christmas; I send cards and birthday texts, and that's about it. My aunt has been a big part of my life. She helped me through the divorce, sat with me when my father was dying and stayed with me for a week after my surgery a few years ago. She has never held the $50,000 over me until now. At dinner last month, she asked me to change my will so the house goes to her two children when I die.

She said it isn't unreasonable and wanted me to consider her offer. She doesn't need the money herself. She just wants her kids to eventually benefit from what she gave me. I told her I'd always understood the money as a gift to me, not an investment in the house or an early inheritance for her children. She had a poker face, but I could tell she did not like my response. I don't want to punish her for being generous. But I'm not comfortable with that request.

I don't want to leave a house worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to two people I barely know. I have no children, and I've always planned for whatever I leave to go to my brother, a dear friend and a couple of charities I care about. I haven't thought of the house as a bargaining chip, just as the biggest thing I own. My aunt says I'm being too literal and that family isn't supposed to keep score. Now I feel gaslighted!

Am I being selfish for refusing to leave the house, or a good part of it, to my aunt's children?

Grateful Homeowner

Related: After 46 years working, I'm not retiring - instead, I take a vacation every month. Is that a good life in your 70s?

You can email The Moneyist with any financial and ethical questions at qfottrell@marketwatch.com. The Moneyist regrets he cannot reply to questions individually.

The $50,000 was a gift, not a loan.

Dear Homeowner,

You are not being selfish. You have agency over your own life and finances. You are not being gaslighted. You are feeling pressured.

The $50,000 was a gift, not a loan and that, to split hairs, is being used as the bargaining chip. You can acknowledge that without agreeing to change your will. If you want to offer something, a modest bequest to her children is a proportionate option. Your aunt may not have meant to have come across so aggressively. Sometimes, people can feel embarrassed in the moment.

If you are uncomfortable about leaving her children any money, don't do it. It's far better to be uncomfortable with your aunt's request and her response to your answer than it is to be uncomfortable with giving money to people you barely know. It's your house - and you can leave it to whom you want to.

What now? Let's assume that $50,000 would be worth $216,000 in 30 years with compounding. You could leave each of her children $108,000, which is more than generous, and reimburses them for the money your aunt gave you out, with interest, assuming that the down payment reduced their inheritance. That's a suggestion, not a request.

You have poured $90,000 into this home to renovate, which has added value; you have worked hard over the last 11 years to pay off the principal and the interest; and you have taken pride in knowing that you have created a home that you can be proud of. Millions of housebuyers get help with a down payment, although it varies by generation.

Homebuyers frequently receive financial help

Four in 10 homeowners received financial help with a down payment on their current home, including nearly 80% of Generation Z homeowners, 56% of millennials and 35% of Generation X (which happens to be your cohort), according to a recent LendingTree survey. The percentage was much lower (12%) for baby boomers.

However, arguably it was easier to buy a house 30 years ago, as the price-to-income ratio has narrowed significantly. Depending on the study, the typical home costs up to seven times the median annual salary today versus just four times the median annual salary 30 years ago. That would explain why fewer baby boomers needed a leg up from parents/family members.

Your aunt definitely overstepped the mark.

Your aunt, for better or for worse, bided her time. You are now in your 50s and never had children of your own, and she has your home in her crosshairs. Yes, she has been a kind and supportive aunt, attending your graduation and helping you get your foot on the property ladder. In many ways, she has been like another mother to you.

If she were your mother, I could see a similar scenario playing out where she would suggest that you support the family cause and leave your house to your brother. But you have no children, and you have already decided to remember your brother in your will, and yet your aunt decided to proffer a version of that request. As an aunt, it doesn't quite land in the same way.

Children often ask the same of their parents

Lest we forget, these pages are rife with adult children, grandchildren, nieces and nephews making similar requests of their elders, asking what will happen to their estate after they're gone, and giving helpful suggestions about what should happen to the estate - which, surprise, surprise! - always seem to favor the one asking the question.

Asking the question is certainly a brazen, if not entirely unusual, state of affairs in families, especially if she considers herself a de facto guardian. However, she definitely overstepped the mark by indicating that leaving the home to her two adult children is the "decent" thing to do. That's a lot more prescriptive than just asking a question.

You don't have to feel ashamed about accepting her gift. Without your aunt's gift, you may never have been able to buy a home or it would have taken you many years. Yes, you are one of the millions of homebuyers receive assistance in the form of a down payment, mortgage payments and/or acting as a guarantor - so her generosity means you are not alone

What do you tell your aunt? You can tell her that you appreciate her help with the down payment, and you will give some thought, but that your estate plans are private. You don't have to answer to anyone. If she persists, you may wish to make it clear that being single and without children does not mean that you have to abide by other people's wishes.

Ultimately, it was a gift, and you can do what you want.

Related: 'We lived within our means': I earned $30,000 as a pastor and still retired comfortably. Why don't you tell people that?

Arrvel Expands Thermal Label Printer Portfolio for Businesses and Everyday Use

Arrvel Expands Thermal Label Printer Portfolio for Businesses and Everyday Use

PR Newswire

SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 10, 2026

SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 10, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Arrvel is expanding its label printing portfolio with thermal printing solutions designed to support e-commerce sellers, small businesses, and everyday labeling needs. Combining compact designs with practical functionality, Arrvel's label printers provide convenient solutions for shipping, inventory management, product identification, and household organization.

As online retail and home-based businesses continue to develop, efficient labeling has become an important part of daily operations. Arrvel's expanded portfolio addresses these needs with dedicated printing solutions that help users manage labeling tasks across business and personal environments without relying on traditional ink-based printers.

Arrvel A42BT: Wireless Thermal Printing for Modern Workflows

A key product in Arrvel's portfolio is the A42BT, a 4×6 Bluetooth thermal shipping label printer designed for online sellers, small businesses, and home offices. Supporting both Bluetooth and USB connectivity, the printer enables users to print from compatible smartphones, tablets, and computers. The FlashLabel Pro app also supports mobile printing, offering greater flexibility for users managing orders and other labeling tasks.

The A42BT delivers print speeds of up to 150 mm/s at 203 DPI resolution. It supports both roll and fanfold labels and accommodates label widths from approximately 1.57 to 4.3 inches, with support for the widely used 4×6-inch shipping label format. These capabilities make the printer suitable for shipping labels, inventory identification, barcodes, and other labeling applications.

Designed for multi-channel sellers, the A42BT is compatible with major e-commerce and shipping platforms, including Amazon, eBay, Shopify, Etsy, and USPS. This compatibility helps users incorporate label printing into their existing order fulfillment workflows.

To learn more about our thermal label printers or make a purchase, explore our thermal label printers on Amazon.

Streamlining Shipping and E-Commerce Operations

Shipping label printing is a fundamental part of order fulfillment for online sellers. As businesses process orders across multiple sales channels, having a dedicated printing solution can help simplify daily workflows, particularly for those operating from home or managing limited workspace.

Arrvel's shipping label printer solutions are designed to integrate into packing stations, home offices, retail counters, and small business environments. By providing a dedicated device for shipping labels, these printers help users organize packaging tasks and prepare orders for dispatch more efficiently.

Their applications extend beyond shipping. Businesses can also use label printers to identify products, track inventory, print barcodes, display pricing information, and organize supplies. These capabilities make label printing a practical part of routine business operations.

Direct Thermal Printing Without Ink Cartridges

Arrvel's thermal printers use direct thermal technology, which produces printed content through heat rather than conventional ink or toner. This method is particularly suitable for labels containing shipping addresses, text, barcodes, and other frequently used information.

Because direct thermal printing does not require ink cartridges or ribbons, it can simplify printer maintenance and reduce the need to replenish traditional printing supplies. For users who regularly produce labels, this offers a straightforward approach to everyday printing.

Arrvel's thermal printing solutions support a variety of applications, from e-commerce fulfillment and logistics to retail operations, office organization, and household labeling. By focusing on dedicated label printing, the company aims to provide practical options for users with different printing requirements.

Beyond Shipping: Supporting Everyday Labeling Needs

Although shipping is a major application for label printers, their functionality extends to many other business and personal tasks. Arrvel's solutions can help users organize information, identify products, and maintain more structured work and living spaces.

Small businesses can use labels for inventory tracking, product identification, packaging, and storage management. At home, users can label boxes, folders, shelves, and containers to make everyday organization easier. Independent sellers and creators can also incorporate printed labels into product packaging and order preparation.

This versatility allows a single label printer to serve multiple purposes, making it a useful tool for businesses and individuals who need a convenient way to create clear, consistent labels for different applications.

Compact Solutions for Modern Workspaces

The growth of remote work, independent businesses, and home-based e-commerce has increased demand for equipment that fits into smaller, more flexible work environments. For many users, printing devices need to occupy minimal space while remaining accessible for routine tasks.

Arrvel develops compact, practical printing solutions that can be integrated into desks, packing stations, retail counters, and home offices. The A42BT reflects this approach, measuring approximately 7.2 × 3.15 × 2.56 inches and weighing about 0.86 lb. Its compact footprint makes it suitable for space-conscious workspaces, including home-based businesses and small-scale shipping operations.

Through its label printing portfolio, Arrvel continues to address everyday labeling requirements with solutions designed around practical functionality, flexible connectivity, and convenient use.

About Arrvel

Arrvel is a brand of Emdoor Information and a global provider of industrial technology solutions, specializing in rugged tablets and label printers for small businesses. Backed by a publicly listed parent company with over ten years of experience, Arrvel integrates advanced R&D, in-house manufacturing, and global logistics to deliver efficient, reliable products to customers worldwide.
